interactions.label: What prevents cardiac muscle from undergoing tetanus, unlike skeletal muscle?

params.question: What prevents cardiac muscle from undergoing tetanus, unlike skeletal muscle?

answers.text: Cardiac cells lack the ability to summate contractions due to their small size

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cardiac cell size is not the reason. Tetanus prevention depends on the electrical refractory period, not cell dimensions.

answers.text: The prolonged refractory period caused by the Phase 2 plateau of the cardiac action potential

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Phase 2 plateau, sustained by L-type calcium channel inflow for 200–300 ms, keeps the cell refractory for about 250 ms — long enough that the muscle relaxes fully before the next action potential can trigger contraction.

answers.text: Continuous parasympathetic inhibition by the vagus nerve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vagal tone slows heart rate but does not prevent tetanus. Even a denervated heart cannot tetanise, because the long refractory period is an intrinsic property of cardiac muscle.

answers.text: Absence of the troponin-tropomyosin complex in cardiac myocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cardiac muscle does contain the troponin-tropomyosin system for contraction. Tetanus prevention is due to the prolonged refractory period, not the contractile protein composition.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is the Phase 2 plateau. L-type calcium channels keep the membrane depolarised for 200–300 ms, giving cardiac muscle a refractory period long enough to prevent summation and tetanus.
Exactly right. The Phase 2 calcium plateau extends the refractory period to approximately 250 ms, ensuring each contraction ends before the next can begin — a built-in safeguard against tetanus.

interactions.label: During auscultation, a third heart sound (S3) is heard in a 60-year-old patient.

params.question: During auscultation, a third heart sound (S3) is heard in a 60-year-old patient. What does this finding most likely indicate?

answers.text: A normal variant related to rapid ventricular filling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: S3 is normal in children and young adults due to rapid ventricular filling, but in adults over 40 it is pathological, not a benign variant.
Aortic stenosis produces a systolic ejection murmur, not a third heart sound. S3 occurs during the rapid filling phase of diastole.
Correct. In adults, S3 results from blood rushing into a dilated, compliant ventricle during rapid filling — a sign of heart failure or volume overload.
Mitral valve prolapse produces a mid-systolic click, not a third heart sound. S3 is a low-pitched diastolic sound.

overallFeedback.feedback: S3 is a low-pitched sound heard during rapid ventricular filling. While normal in children, in adults it signals heart failure — blood rushing into a dilated ventricle that cannot empty adequately.
Well done. S3 occurs during rapid ventricular filling in diastole. While normal in children, in adults it strongly suggests ventricular dysfunction or volume overload.

params.question: Cannon 'a' waves in the jugular venous pulse are a characteristic finding in atrial fibrillation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract in an organised fashion, so 'a' waves are absent from the JVP. Cannon 'a' waves occur in complete heart block, where the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve because atrial and ventricular rhythms are dissociated.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Cannon 'a' waves occur in complete heart block, when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve. In atrial fibrillation, coordinated atrial contraction is absent, so 'a' waves disappear entirely from the JVP.

interactions.label: Why does the atrioventricular (AV) node delay the cardiac impulse for approximat

params.question: Why does the atrioventricular (AV) node delay the cardiac impulse for approximately 0.1 seconds?

answers.text: To allow atrial contraction to complete and fill the ventricles before they contract

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 0.1-second delay ensures the atria have enough time to contract and push the final 20–30% of blood (the atrial kick) into the ventricles before ventricular systole begins.

answers.text: To allow the SA node to recover before the next impulse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SA node recovery occurs independently and is not dependent on AV node conduction time. The delay serves a haemodynamic purpose, not a pacemaker recovery function.

answers.text: To synchronise the right and left bundle branches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bundle branch synchronisation occurs downstream in the His-Purkinje system. The AV delay exists specifically to allow sequential atrial-then-ventricular contraction.

answers.text: To prevent retrograde conduction back into the atria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the AV node does limit retrograde conduction, the primary physiological purpose of the 0.1-second delay is to ensure the atria empty before the ventricles contract.

overallFeedback.feedback: The AV node holds the impulse for 0.1 seconds so the atria can complete their contraction (the atrial kick) and fill the ventricles before ventricular systole begins. This delay appears as the PR interval on the ECG.
Exactly. Without this delay, the ventricles would contract before the atria finish emptying — losing the atrial kick and reducing stroke volume by up to 20–30%.

interactions.label: The sinoatrial node has an intrinsic firing rate of approximately 100 beats per

params.question: The sinoatrial node has an intrinsic firing rate of approximately 100 beats per minute, yet the resting heart rate is around 70. What accounts for this difference?

answers.text: Circulating adrenaline suppresses the SA node at rest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Circulating adrenaline acts on beta-1 receptors to increase heart rate, not decrease it. At rest, adrenaline levels are low and do not suppress the SA node.

answers.text: The Bainbridge reflex reduces heart rate when venous return is low

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Bainbridge reflex is triggered by increased venous return and causes tachycardia, not bradycardia. It does not explain the lower resting heart rate.

answers.text: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor downregulation occurs at rest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-1 receptor downregulation is not a normal resting mechanism. The lower resting heart rate is due to active parasympathetic inhibition, not receptor changes.

answers.text: Tonic vagal activity slows the SA node via acetylcholine acting on M2 muscarinic receptors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The vagus nerve is tonically active at rest, releasing acetylcholine that acts on M2 muscarinic receptors. This slows Phase 4 depolarisation, reducing the firing rate from the intrinsic ~100 to approximately 70 bpm.

overallFeedback.feedback: The vagus nerve is tonically active at rest, continuously releasing acetylcholine onto M2 receptors at the SA node. This slows Phase 4 depolarisation, bringing the heart rate down from the node's intrinsic ~100 to roughly 70 bpm.
Well done. Vagal dominance at rest is why atropine — which blocks muscarinic receptors — causes immediate tachycardia. It removes the brake that normally holds the SA node below its intrinsic rate.
